title: Effect of sequential tempering on the microstructural and mechanical properties of the 7075-alloy after a two-step aging treatment at 105 °C and 140 °C
abstract: Abstract In the present work, the influence of the heating rate on the precipitation kinetics of an Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy (AA7075) and its subsequent effect on mechanical properties was investigated. Microhardness and tensile tests were used to examine the hardening and plastic characteristics of the alloy. Transmission and scanning electron microscopy were used to analyze the alloy’s microstructural development. The Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy showed notable alterations in microstructure and mechanical behavior during different aging phases. High ductility was a characteristic of the microstructure upon quenching. A high-volume fraction of fine precipitates is visible in the alloy after it has aged at 140 °C, which is the maximum hardness value. The volume fraction of these fine precipitates was quantitatively estimated to be approximately ~ 8–10%. The minimum hardening is recorded after aging at 350 °C. The radical change in the microstructure of the alloy influences its mechanical behavior, especially in hardening and plasticity. By reducing the heating rate, the yield strength is further increased, and the elongation is almost the same. Moreover, a sufficient nucleation of  η ′ can be achieved as the heating rate decreases, and as a result, the improvement in mechanical properties is also very significant.
journal: Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The Al–Mg alloy system has been widely used in the automotive, electronics, aerospace, defense, and gasoline industries [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ] due to its exceptional resistance, high heat and electric conductivity, and weldability. Similarly, high-strength Al–Zn–Mg alloys such as AA7075 are extensively employed in aerospace and structural applications due to their superior strength-to-mass ratio, particularly when processed under T6 and T7x tempering conditions that optimize precipitation hardening and mechanical performance [ 4 ,  5 ,  6 ,  7 ,  8 – 9 ]. It can be processed into components with a range of geometries, including sheets, rods, tubes, and wires [ 10 ]. Mg is one of the key alloying elements for solid solution strengthening of Al alloys. The addition of Mg can effectively improve the corrosion resistance [ 2 ] and mechanical properties [ 3 ] of Al alloys. In AA7075 alloys, Mg acts synergistically with Zn to form strengthening precipitates (MgZn 2 ), which are highly sensitive to heat treatment routes such T6 (peak-aged) and T7x (over-aged) tempers, thereby controlling the balance between strength and corrosion resistance [ 5 ,  6 ,  8 ]. The  α -Al phase precipitates first as coarse dendrites during thermodynamic solidification, and then, additional phases precipitate between the dendrites and around the grain boundary. Magnesium is highly soluble in aluminum, reaching mass percentages of 17.4 at% at 450 °C and 16.4 at% at 270 °C, respectively. As the cooling process proceeds, the solubility of magnesium in aluminum drastically declines and is also influenced by the pace of cooling. The lattice constant of Al increases by 5 × 10 –13  m for every 1 at% increase in the solid solubility of Mg in Al due to the significant diameter difference between the two atoms, with the latter being 13 at% bigger than the former [ 3 ,  11 ]. Therefore, adding a lot of magnesium atoms to Al alloys strengthens them in solid solution. The crystallographic lattice constant at the equilibrium solution threshold value may be 4.1294 × 10 –10  m, and the ultimate tensile strength may increase by 33 MPa. When the addition of magnesium surpasses 5–6 at%, segregation of  β -Al 3 Mg 2  phases is produced. Low ductility of the Al alloys is easily caused by the very brittle character of such  β -Al 3 Mg 2  phases at 327 °C. Furthermore, the formation of big grains is facilitated by the low nuclei density of precipitates, which somewhat strengthens the material because the solubility of magnesium in aluminum drastically reduces with cooling. According to Lee et al. [ 12 ], the solute’s magnesium atoms fill gaps in the Al matrix, creating strong obstacles to dislocation movement and resulting in high tensile strength and poor elongation throughout the deformation process. A comparable strengthening mechanism is observed in AA7075 alloys, where dislocation motion is strongly hindered by fine  η ′ precipitates formed during T6 tempering, while coarser  η  precipitates formed during T7x tempering reduce strength but enhance stress corrosion cracking resistance [ 4 ,  8 ,  9 ]. Because of this, Al–Mg frequently has poor formability at room temperature, especially when the Mg content is high. Likewise, AA7075-T6 exhibits limited formability at room temperature, which has motivated the development of alternative forming strategies and heat treatments to improve ductility without significantly compromising strength [ 8 ,  9 ]. Such Al–Mg alloys must be processed at high temperatures, which significantly raises the cost of manufacture [ 13 ,  14 ].

In the past few decades, a lot of research has been done on the effects of various alloying elements, such as manganese, silicon, scandium, iron, titanium, and zirconium. The goal was to increase corrosion resistance and strength in the heat-affected zone by creating hardening precipitates. However, the results showed that Zn showed a decrease in corrosion resistance, primarily in the heat-affected zone, especially as it aged. This behavior is particularly critical in AA7075 alloys, where Zn-rich precipitates contribute to high strength but also increase susceptibility to localized corrosion, especially in the peak-aged T6 temper condition [ 5 ,  7 ]. While the addition of Zr to Al–Mg alloys showed an exponential improvement in elongation of 350% at temperatures of 500 °C, the properties of the intermetallic had a major impact on the superplastic behavior of Al–Mg alloys [ 15 ]. Additionally, adding Sc and Zr at the same time is a useful strategy that can greatly increase the strength of Al–Mg alloys by creating core–shell Al 3 (Sc, Zr) precipitates [ 16 ,  17 – 18 ]. In high-strength Al–Zn–Mg alloys such as AA7075, minor additions of Zr and Sc are also employed to form thermally stable dispersoids that inhibit recrystallization and improve mechanical performance during thermomechanical processing [ 4 ]. According to thermal history, Zr additions to aluminum alloys may result in the formation of metastable Al 3 Zr-dispersoids [ 19 ], and Al 3 Zr dispersoids have a significant impact on the refinement of grain structure, thermal stability, and mechanical properties like tensile strength, ductility, and yield strength [ 20 ,  21 – 22 ]. Zirconium is found to be 0.28 at% soluble in aluminum at temperatures of 660 °C.

This precipitation sequence is particularly well-established in AA7075 alloys and its strongly influenced by tempering conditions such as T6 and T7x, where the size, distribution, and coherency of  η ′ and  η  precipitates govern the resulting mechanical and corrosion properties [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ]. After a solution treatment and a lower temperature quenching, the  α -sss is produced. The excess vacancy concentration has a significant impact on the decomposition process, making it susceptible to the quenching condition [ 30 ]. According to previous works [ 25 ,  27 ,  31 ,  32 ], GP zones are defined as ordered and coherent layers of Zn and Mg/Al atoms on {1 0 0}Al that typically show small spherical morphology precipitates. There has been a lot of research interest in the development process of these zones [ 24 ,  27 ] as well as the composition [ 33 ,  34 ,  35 – 36 ], structure, and features of GP zones [ 37 ]. It was thought that the degree of vacancy supersaturation had a significant influence on their development. They have a {1 1 1} habitual plane, are entirely consistent with the matrix, and form before the  η ′. Due to the finer dispersion inside the grain during the aging process following quenching from a solution treatment temperature, this intermediate phase primarily aids in the alloy’s age hardening. The exact crystallographic structure, orientation, and composition of the metastable  η ′ phase are still in question, although they have been studied now because of the importance of structure in nucleation and growth. For the  η ′ phase, several structural hypotheses have been put forth, including orthorhombic [ 38 ], monoclinic [ 39 ], and hexagonal [ 31 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ]. Up to nine orientations are known to occur during the equilibrium g phase [ 43 ]. This incoherent phase manifests itself in the later stages of aging. In over-aged tempers such as T7x, the transformation from  η ’ to coarse  η  precipitates leads to a reduction in strength but significantly improves resistance to stress corrosion cracking, which is critical for aerospace applications of AA7075 [ 4 ,  5 ]. Moreover, complicated cubic precipitate T (Mg 32 (Al,Zn) 49 ) may also form in alloys with quite high Mg concentrations. It is commonly known that an alloy’s microstructure plays a crucial role in its mechanical characteristics. The creation of high-performance industrial alloys necessitates a quantitative prediction of the microstructure to better understand the relationship between mechanical parameters (such as toughness, yield stress, and work hardening rate) and processing (thermomechanical treatments) [ 44 ,  45 ,  46 ,  47 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ]. In this context, tailoring heat treatments such as T6 and T7x in AA7075 alloys is essential to achieve an optimal compromise between strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance, depending on service requirements [ 4 ,  8 ]. It is well known that the ductility and yield stress are inversely related, with the minimum ductility and maximum age hardening occurring at the same time. Thus, the present work aims to determine the suitable heat treatment for a better compromise between these two terms. Meanwhile, the importance of the heating temperature rise rate in improving mechanical properties is being studied. Particular attention is given to the influence of multi-step and sequential tempering strategies, which have shown promise in refining precipitate distributions and enhancing the performance of AA7075 alloys beyond conventional T6 treatments.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs: An Al–Zn–Mg alloy was the material produced in this investigation. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICPOES) was used to analyze it. Table  1  provides the chemical composition. Following a 24-h solution treatment at 475 °C and quenching in ice water media, an 84-h natural aging process was carried out. Table 1 Chemical composition of the investigated Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy (mass%) Al Zn Mg Cu Mn Fe Si Ti Cr Zr Balance 5.7 2.5 1.7 0.23 0.28 0.26 0.05 0.19 0.18

Table  2  summarizes the thermal histories and processing parameters of all samples (S1–S6), derived from the same AA7075 alloy to ensure identical chemical composition and initial conditions. All samples were solution-treated at 475 °C for 24 h, quenched in ice water, and subjected to different aging routes, including sing-stage aging, two-stage aging with intermediate quenching, and sequential tempering with controlled heating rates. Subsequently, sequential tempering treatments were performed using programmable furnace equipped with PID controller to ensure precise control of the heating rates between the different tempering stages. The temperature evolution was monitored using calibrated K-type thermocouples positioned in close proximity to the samples to accurately capture the effective thermal history, with an accuracy of approximately ± 1–2 °C. Table 2 Summary of thermal histories and processing parameters of samples S1–S6, derived from the same AA7075 alloy Sample Solution treatment Natural aging First aging step (105 °C) Quenching between steps Heating rate to 140 °C/K h −1 Second aging step (140 °C) S1 475 °C/24 h  + ice quench Yes No – – 140 °C/4 h S2 475 °C/24 h  + ice quench Yes 105 °C/12 h Yes – 140 °C/4 h S3 475 °C/24 h  + ice quench Yes 105 °C/12 h No 60 140 °C/4 h S4 475 °C/24 h  + ice quench Yes 105 °C/12 h No 30 140 °C/4 h S5 475 °C/24 h + ice quench Yes 105 °C/12 h No 20 140 °C/4 h S6 475 °C/24 h + ice quench Yes 105 °C/12 h No 10 140 °C/4 h

A Shimadzu HVM-2000 hardness tester was used to evaluate Vickers microhardness (Hv) with a load of 500 g applied for 15 s. The results presented here are the average of at least ten measurements. The surfaces of the specimens were physically ground and chemically polished using a combination of 6% HNO 3 , 4% HF, 10% H 3 PO 4 , and 80% H 2 O in preparation for optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) studies. Energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used to perform electron microanalysis at the specimens’ surface after SEM images. It should be noted that EDS analysis was limited to the matrix composition, as its spatial resolution is not sufficient for reliable characterization of nanometric η’ precipitates. Mechanical polishing was used to create thin foils for the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) investigations. A JEM-2000FX transmission electron microscope running at a 200 kV accelerating voltage was used to investigate them. The quantitative volume fraction of precipitates was estimated from TEM images using the point-counting method on at five representative micrographs. ImageJ analysis software was used to measure the precipitate area fraction, which was assumed to approximate the volume fraction.

Tensile tests were conducted using the E-8M standard from the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM). The longitudinal (L) orientation, or parallel to the rolling direction, was used to take the specimens. At room temperature and with a constant strain rate (10 –4  s −1 ), the samples were distorted. Each specimen underwent three tensile tests to guarantee the reliability of the tensile results. Direct machining of the solution-treated and quenched samples produced the tensile specimens. The specimens measured 70 mm in length, 20 mm in width, and 6 mm in thickness. Thermal analyses were performed by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) using a PerkinElmer 30 device of Mettler Toledo calorimeter with a heating/cooling rate of 10 K min –1  under argon atmosphere in a temperature range of 35–550 C.

sections.heading: One-step aging
paragraphs: Figure  1  represents the microhardness HV evolution as a function of temperature for the investigated samples aged for 2 h and quenched in cold water. At lower aging temperatures (typically ≤ 140 °C), microhardness increases. This increase may be explained by the optimal precipitation of fine, coherent  η ′ phase particles [ 51 ]. Indeed, maximum microhardness is achieved at the optimal temperature 140 °C for 2 h aging, because of these fine precipitates, finely distributed and coherent, offering maximum strengthening. In other words, these fine particles impede dislocation motion, resulting in peak hardness. But, in the under-tempering stage, the curve shows a decrease in hardness at 105 °C before reaching the main hardening peak at 140 °C. This decrease may be related to the formation of the maximum of GP zones, which are known to form during early aging in Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloys [ 46 ,  56 ,  57 ] (no direct quantification of GP zones was performed in the present study). Moreover, previous works reported that copper stabilizes GP zones [ 52 ,  53 ] and slows down the growth kinetics [ 46 ]. Moreover, Smith and Grant [ 54 ] stated that copper increases the nucleation rate, subsequently increasing the density of precipitates and their volume fraction; for this reason, the microhardness values of quaternary alloys are higher than those of the ternary alloy. In copper-containing alloys, although copper atoms are evidently present in the composition of the  η ′ and  η -phases most of the time [ 55 ,  56 ,  57 ,  58 – 59 ], it is not entirely clear what types of GP zones are formed. More recent studies propose that these zones exist in two distinct forms [ 60 ,  61 ]. The  η ′ phase is responsible for the maximum hardening, it has a hexagonal structure [ 62 ,  63 ], and a Mg/Zn ratio is between 0.7 and 0.9 [ 63 ]. It is consistent with the matrix and stable in the temperature range (120–150 °C). It has been reported that the stability range of the GP zones and the content of  η ′ precipitate increase with the copper content of the alloys. These particles are abundant (10 16 –10 17  cm −3 ), precipitate in the form of very thin platelets parallel to the {111}Al planes, and their thicknesses vary between 2 and 50 nm [ 64 ]. Fig. 1 Microhardness–temperature curve for the AA7075-alloy aged for 2 h after quenching in ice water

For significant structural hardening, the formation of a high density and the homogeneity of distribution of clusters and/or metastable precipitates in the matrix are sought. In structural hardening, the volume fraction of fine precipitates can reach 4 or 5% in the case of 7000 series alloys. According to Rym [ 65 ], the formation of a high density of clusters and/or metastable precipitates in a ternary alloy is respected if the main addition elements have relative atomic radius deviations of opposite signs compared to that of aluminum, which would tend to minimize the elastic energy of distortion of the network introduced by the formation of clusters and would therefore favor the nucleation of precipitates. The Al–Zn–Mg and Al–Zn–Mg–Cu systems are interesting examples ready to undergo significant structural hardening, since they consist of at least one addition element with a small atomic radius (Zn and/or Cu) and one element with a large atomic radius (Mg).

At temperatures between 180 and 350 °C, the curve drops, indicating a progressive decrease in hardness up to its minimum value at 350 °C. At this interval of temperatures, the over-aging precipitates coarsen and/or transform to stable, incoherent η (MgZn 2 ) Phase. Nevertheless, coarser particles are less efficient at blocking dislocations, resulting in a reduction in hardness. Yet, the proportion of coarse precipitates that can embrittle the grain boundaries and diminish the solid solution (precipitation on dispersoids) is influenced by the quenching rate. While no precipitate is visible on the dispersoid following a fast quench, a slow quench may result in extensive nucleation of precipitates on the dispersoids following the solution treatment, which lowers the amount of solute available for fine-scale precipitation and, consequently, the hardening potential [ 66 ,  67 ].

The SEM image of AA7075 alloy, which was maintained at 475 °C for 24 h, quenched in ice water, treated for 3.5 days, and aged at 140 °C, is given in Fig.  2 . Figure  2 a specifically shows the general microstructure at low magnification, highlighting the total distribution of precipitates within the matrix. The micrograph shows the high density and well-distributed fine precipitates that cause the hardening peak observed in Fig.  1 . In fact, they are actual barriers that impede the dislocation movement. The corresponding EDS analysis indicates that the precipitates generated from this treatment are composed of Mg, Cu, Zn, and Al. The quantitative evaluation of these precipitates is complicated since it is far more difficult to ascertain their exact chemical formula. At high magnification (× 1000), two distinct kinds of intermetallic particles were visible (see Fig.  2 ). Figures  2 b corresponds to the SEM image at higher magnification with marked zones selected for EDS analysis, while Fig.  2 c presents the corresponding EDS spectrum of a specific analyzed region. Fig. 2 SEM micrographs and EDS analyses for AA7075 alloy aged at 140 °C:  a  low-magnification SEM image,  b  high-magnification SEM image with marked regions for compositional analysis and the EDS analysis of white precipitates, and  c  EDS spectrum of the black precipitates

The white particles are essentially composed of the elements Cu, Fe, and Al (Fig.  2 b). These precipitates may consist of Al 2 CuMg(S) or Al 7 Cu 2 Fe [ 68 ]. The black precipitates have a high concentration of Si and Mg, which gives information on the chemical formula Mg 2 Si (Fig.  2 c). Dense and consistent GP zones are necessary for significant hardening since they are known to be very efficient germs for  η ′ precipitates and because maximum hardening maximizes the precipitation of  η ′ phases. Therefore, we tempered first at the temperature where the largest GP zones form, and then, we tempered at the temperature where the  η ′ precipitates are optimized.

sections.heading: Two-step aging
paragraphs: Figure  3  schematically illustrates the two distinct sequential tempering routes applied to the 7075 alloy. In the first route (Fig.  3 a), the alloy is initially aged at 105 °C for 12 h (First stage), followed by quenching in ice water, and subsequently re-aged at 140 °C for 4 h (second stage). This intermediate quenching step introduces a clear thermal discontinuity between the two aging stages. For clarity, the sample aged only at 140 °C is denoted S1, while the sample subjected to 105 °C aging, quenching, and subsequent aging at 140 °C is designed S2. In contrast, the second route (Fig.  3 b) involves a mountainous two-stage tempering process without interruption. After aging at 105 °C for 12 h, the temperature is progressively increased to 140 °C at a controlled heating rate, eliminating any quenching step and ensuring a smooth thermal transition between the two stages. The alloy is then held at 140 °C for 4 h to investigate the influence of the heating rate during this transition, four rates (10, 20, 30, and 60 K h −1 ) were applied, corresponding S6, S5, S4, and S3, respectively. This approach enables a direct comparison between discontinuous (quenched) and continuous (rate-controlled) transitions from 105 to 140 °C, thereby clarifying the role of thermal path on precipitation evolution and the resulting mechanical performance in Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloys system. Fig. 3 Schematic description of the first and second types of tempering in the bi-level of alloy 7075

sections.heading: DSC investigation
paragraphs: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was employed to probe the thermal stability and transformation behavior of intermediate precipitates in the 7075 alloy over defined temperature ranges, using samples representing distinct metallurgical states. As shown in the curve (Fig.  4 ), several exothermic and endothermic peaks are observed (colored zones). According to the literature [ 23 ,  24 ,  25 ,  26 ,  27 ,  28 – 29 ], the exothermic peaks are associated with precipitation reactions, whereas the endothermic peaks correspond to the dissolution of various precipitate phases. The DSC curve of the quenched condition reveals a sequence of thermal events characteristic of Al–Mg–Zn–Cu systems. An initial weak exothermic peak observed around ~ 100 °C may be attributed to the formation of Guinier–Preston (GP) zones from the supersaturated solid solution [ 69 ,  70 ]. This is followed by more pronounced exothermic peak near ~ 200 °C, corresponding to the precipitation of the metastable  η ′ phase, which plays a key role in strengthening [ 34 ]. At the intermediate temperature (~ 250–320 °C), an endothermic region is detected, indicating the dissolution of the GP zones and  η ′ precipitate [ 40 ]. Subsequently, a broad exothermic peak extending from ~ 320 to 450 °C is associated with the formation and growth of the stable  η  (MgZn2) phase [ 71 ]. A distinct double exothermic peak observed in the temperature range of approximately 470–500 °C is attributed to overlapping precipitation-related processes. The first peak is associated with the reprecipitation of  η  or transition phases following prior dissolution, resulting from the re-establishment of a supersaturated solid solution, while the second peak corresponds to the subsequent growth, coarsening, and stabilization of these precipitates. The splitting of this peak reflects the complex precipitation kinetics and the sequential nature of nucleation and growth process in Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloys [ 60 ,  72 ]. At higher temperatures (> 500 °C), a strong endothermic reaction observed, corresponding to the dissolution of equilibrium precipitates and re-establishment of a solid solution [ 1 ]. These results provide direct thermal evidence of the precipitation sequence and strongly support the interpretation of the microstructural evolution during subsequent aging and tempering treatments. Fig. 4 DSC curves of Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy (AA7075) at quenching state

sections.heading: First type of two-stage tempering
paragraphs: The AA7075 alloy, which was quenched in ice water, aged for 3.5 days, and aged at 140 °C, has a hardness of 222.17 HV. The hardness of the alloy aged in two stages (named S 2 ) was measured to be around 231.11 HV. The difference revealed in the hardness measurement shows the benefit of two-stage tempering. Figure  4  illustrates the superposition of the tensile curves of these samples. The tensile results are promising; therefore, by a two-step tempering, an increase in the yield strength is observed, and the alloy maintains a comparable elongation. Indeed, the yield strength increases from 496.75 to 551.89 MPa, and the elongation remains unchanged at 18.20%. Pre-aging at 105 °C may cause a high nucleation rate and the creation of multiple GP zones [ 46 ]. At higher temperatures, specifically 140 °C, the fine precipitate’s dispersion is then preserved. Therefore, these fine precipitates trapped by quenching and, by subsequent tempering, are then transformed to the second aging temperature at 140 °C, where the maximum hardening is obtained. However, the increase in yield strength given by two-stage tempering may be related to the higher density of precipitate, leading to a smaller inter-precipitate spacing by requiring a higher force to allow the movement of dislocations [ 73 ]. Indeed, fine and dense precipitates constitute effective obstacles that hinder the movement of dislocations.

sections.heading: Second type of two-stage tempering
paragraphs: As shown in Fig.  3 b, this second type of two-stage tempering is distinguished from the first type by the absence of quenching between the two stages. To reach the temperature of the second stage, we varied the rise rate. The measured microhardness value of AA7075 alloy, in the case of a heating rate equal to 60 °C h −1 , is of the order of 236.73 HV. This increase in microhardness compared to that measured after aging at 105 °C, quenching, and a second aging at 140 °C of the same alloy may be due to obtaining a higher volume fraction of hardening precipitates. Indeed, quenching is a very delicate operation, and we must take several precautions to make it as fast as possible to trap the maximum number of vacancies and achieve a high nucleation rate. Ungár et al. [ 74 ] showed that  η ′ hardening precipitates germinate on GP zones from 100 °C. In the present work, we found the maximum of the GP zones at 105 °C (Fig.  5 ). With this type of treatment, we try to transform as much as possible of the GP zones formed during tempering at 105 °C into the  η ′-hardening phases’ at 140 °C. In fact, the precipitation germs and the GP zones play an important role in hardening at higher temperatures. Fig. 5 Tensile curves of alloy 7075 samples; (S1) aged at 140 °C, (S2) aged at 105 °C, quenched and at 140 °C and (S3), (S4), (S5), and (S6): aged at 105 °C and at 140 °C at a heating rate of 60 °C h −1 , 30 °C h −1 , 20 °C h −1 , and 10 °C h −1 , respectively

Tensile tests are used to study the influence of the temperature rise rate on the precipitation kinetics of AA7075 alloy and subsequently on its mechanical properties. In Fig.  5 , we have combined the tensile curve of the sample aged at 140 °C and those of the samples aged in two stages. As shown, the influence of the temperature rise rate is very strong in this alloy. The superposition of the tensile curves of the sample aged only at 140 °C (S1) and the sample aged in two stages, at a heating rate equal to 60 °C h −1  (S3), shows that the yield strength of sample S3 is 585.24 MPa, improved by 88.49 MPa compared to the single-stage aged state, and the alloy lost only 0.3% of its elongation. To transform a larger volume fraction of the GP zones into  η ′ hardening phases, we tried to slow down this transformation reaction by decreasing the temperature rise rate; the superposition of the tensile curves of the sample aged at 140 °C and the sample aged in two stages, at a temperature rise rate equal to 30 °C h −1 , proves this result. In fact, by reducing the heating rate, the yield strength is further increased, and the elongation is almost the same. The results obtained from the tensile tests confirm the hardness measurement of the sample aged for 12 h at 105 °C and 4 h at 140 °C at a heating rate of 30 °C h −1 , i.e., 240.21 HV.

The composition of the alloy controls the extent of the overlap domain. Indeed, the nucleation of  η ′ would thus begin before the end of the reversion of the GP, for zinc contents greater than 2.5 atomic% [ 75 ]. Our alloy is one of the alloys cited where the Zn content is greater than 2.5 at.%. Since in the case of quaternary alloys, the Cu element would have a beneficial influence by stabilizing the  η ′ phase [ 76 ] and by widening the overlap domain between the two hardening precipitates, the GP and  η ′ zones [ 54 ]. For that, we tried to sweep this entire domain by further reducing the heating rate. Consequently, the hardness measured for a sample heated at 20 °C h −1  to reach the second stage is 241.72 HV. Moreover, the tensile tests of samples S1 and S5 demonstrate a significant increase in the yield strength (by 122.06 MPa) when the temperature rise rate is reduced to 20 °C h −1 .

Deschamps et al. [ 46 ] showed using DSC that we can clearly see a peak of appearance of  η ′ followed by a peak of transformation of  η ′ into  η  with a gradual temperature increase. The respective temperatures of these two peaks are 120 and 170 °C. The peaks of  η ′ and the transformation of  η ′ into  η . On the other hand, they are nearly overlaid and arise at a lower temperature with a rapid temperature increase, suggesting a more challenging nucleation of  η ′. As a result, they discovered that GP zones dissolve more readily during rapid heating than during moderate heating. This aligns with our findings. By increasing the temperature gradually, we prevent the conversion of  η ′ to  η  from accelerating and maintain the maximum number of GP zones, which are essential for a proper nucleation of  η ′ precipitates. A slower temperature increases no longer results in improved hardening. As shown in Fig.  5 , when the sample is heated at 10 °C h −1 , its yield strength is almost equal to that found when it is heated at 20 °C h −1 . Sha and Cerezo [ 77 ] showed that after aging the 7050 alloy (Al–Zn–Mg–Cu) at 121 °C for 12 h, only 17% of the GP zones remain. However, after aging the same alloy at the same temperature for only 4 h, the  η ′ - hardening phases present 72% of the precipitates. These results agree with our present work: The maximum of the GP zones is recorded at 105 °C; then, these zones transform into harder  η ′ - phases, and the hardening potential is found at 140 °C.

sections.heading: Determination of the work hardening exponent n
paragraphs: The work hardening index  n  of the single-stage aged sample and those aged in two stages are shown in Fig.  6 . All these indices are low and remain comparable, indicating saturation of hardening and average ductility. Fig. 6 Work hardening indices of 7075 samples aged in one stage:  a  S1 and in two stages:  b  S2,  c  S3,  d  S4,  e  S5, and  f  S6

We note a slight increase in the work hardening index followed by a decrease at a heating rate of 20 °C h −1 . This trend appears to be due to the precipitates becoming increasingly shear, and then saturation is reached. A summary of the mechanical properties of AA7075 alloy is shown in Table  3 . Table 3 Summary of the mechanical properties (microhardness, ultimate tensile strength, yield strength, work hardening exponent ( n ), and elongation) of AA7075 alloy after staged tempering Microhardness ± 4HV Ultimate tensile strength ± 12 MPa Yield Strength ± 10 Mpa Work hardening exponent (n) ± 0.01 Elongation ± 0.8% S 1 222.17 615.38 496.75 0.082 18.21 S 2 231.11 688.08 551.89 0.085 18.19 S 3 236.73 723.02 585.24 0.089 17.91 S 4 240.21 734.06 607.38 0.093 17.98 S 5 241.72 753.20 618.81 0.078 17.72 S 6 242.03 746.11 616.80 0.072 17.53

The evolution of the work hardening exponent (n) with heating rate provides additional insight into the deformation mechanisms governing the alloy. As shown, n slightly increases from 0.082 (S1) to a maximum of 0.093 (S4), followed by a decrease to 0.072 (S6). The initial increase in (n) can be attributed to the formation of a high density of finely distributed GP zones and  η ′ precipitates, which promote strong and homogeneous interaction with dislocations, thereby enhancing strain hardening capacity [ 46 ,  57 ,  79 ]. At this stage, dislocation motion is predominantly controlled by precipitate shearing mechanisms, which contribute to sustained work hardening. However, as the heating rate decreases further (S4 → S6), the slight reduction in (n) is associated with coarsening and increased spacing of precipitates, leading to a transition toward dislocation bypassing (Orowan looping). This mechanism reduces the accumulation of dislocations and consequently lowers the work hardening capability. The relatively low and narrow range of (n) values (0.072–0.093) suggests limited variation in ductility, consistent with nearly constant elongation values observed.

Quantitatively, the influence of stepped tempering is clearly significant in improving the mechanical properties of AA7075 alloy. Indeed, we were able to increase the yield strength, and the alloy retains its ductility. However, considering the reported standard deviations (Table  3 ), the variations in elongation (on the order of 0.3–0.7%) are within the experimental scatter, indicating that the ductility can be considered statistically unchanged across different conditions. This behavior suggests that the applied tempering treatments enhance strength without significant compromising plasticity. In contrast, the observed increase in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength exceeds the associated standard deviations, confirming that the strengthening effect is statistically significant. The improvement in strength is mainly attributed to the increased density and optimized distribution of  η ′ precipitates, particularly for lower heating rates [ 46 ,  66 ]. These results are consistent with typical AA7075 tempers, where peak-aged conditions (T6) provide high strength, while over-aged conditions (T7x) reduce strength; the present tempering strategy offers a favorable balance between these properties. The effect of heating rate on yield strength exhibits a clear increasing trend as the heating rate decreases from S3 to S6, with yield strength rising significantly from 585.24 to 616.80 MPa, respectively, corresponding to an increase of approximately 32 MPa. This substantial improvement confirms a strong promoting effect of reduced heating rate on precipitation strengthening. However, a further decrease in heating rate (S4 → S5 → S6) results in only minor variations., with yield strength values of 607.38 MPa (S4), 618.81 MPa (S5), and 616.80 MPa (S6). The difference between S4 and S4 (~ 9 MPa) remains within the experimental scatter, indicating that the strengthening effect reaches a saturation regime at S4 (20 °C h −1 ). A similar evolution is observed for microhardness, which increases markedly from 222 HV (S1) to 240 HV (S4), followed by only a marginal change up to 242 HV (S6). Therefore, an improvement in mechanical properties is significant up to S4, whereas the variation between S4 and lower heating rates (S5–S6) can be considered negligible.

The role of Cu in Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloys can be better understood by comparing the present results with reported data for ternary Al-Zn-Mg systems. In Cu-free Al–Zn–Mg alloys, peak-aged conditions typically exhibit hardness values in the range of ~ 130–150 HV and yield strength around 300–420 MPa, depending on composition and aging route, with a relatively sharp peak associated mainly with GP zones and  η ′ precipitation. In contrast, AA 7075 (Al–Zn–Mg–Cu) alloys under comparable T6-type conditions generally reach higher hardness levels of 170–190 HV and yield strengths 500–570 MPa, reflecting the additional contribution of Cu in increasing precipitate density and stabilizing  η ′ phases [ 56 ,  57 ]. Moreover, ternary alloys often show a narrow aging response, whereas quaternary alloys exhibit a broader and more gradual transition in hardness evolution with temperature, consistent with wider precipitation overlap domain. In the present work, significantly higher mechanical properties were obtained, with microhardness values ranging from 220–240 HV, ultimate tensile strength of 600–740 MPa, and yield strength of 500–600 MPa, confirming a strong precipitation hardening response. These values are higher than typical Cu-free Al-Zn-Mg alloys and are slightly higher than standard AA7075-T6 reported in literature, suggesting that Cu contributes to the enhanced strengthening response.

sections.heading: Microstructure after two-stage tempering
paragraphs: TEM micrographs of the one-step and two-stage aged samples are given in Fig.  7 . In contrast to the qualitative description provided previously, a quantitative image analysis was performed to evaluate the precipitate size distribution and number density. The measurements were carried out using multiple representative micrographs for each condition to ensure statistical reliability. The results indicate that the two-step aged samples exhibit significantly higher number density of  η ′ precipitates compared to the single-step aged condition. Specially, the average precipitate size decreases while the number density increases with decreasing heating rate during the transition from 105 to 140 °C. This trend reflects enhanced nucleation kinetics at lower heating rates, which promote the formation of a larger population of fine, uniformly distributed  η ′ precipitates [ 67 ]. Quantitatively, the reduction in precipitate size (D) combined with an increase in number density (Nv ~ 8–10%) leads to a higher obstacle density for dislocation motion. This microstructural refinement directly correlates with the measured increase in microhardness and tensile strength. According to precipitation strengthening theory, the resistance to dislocation motion scales inversely with interparticle spacing, which decreases as precipitate density increases [ 80 ,  81 ]. Consequently, samples processed at lower heating rates exhibit superior mechanical properties due to a finer and more closely spaced precipitate distribution. Furthermore, the precipitates are predominantly spherical to slightly ellipsoidal in morphology and remain homogeneously distributed throughout the matrix in the two-stage aged samples. The high-volume fraction and refined dispersion achieved throughout controlled heating enhance the effectiveness of dislocation pinning, thereby increasing the stress required for dislocation bypass via the Orowan looping mechanism [ 82 ]. As result, these quantitative TEM observations establish a clear microstructure property relationship, demonstrating that the controlled sequential tempering, particularly with reduced heating rates promotes the formation of a dense population of fine  η ′ precipitates, which is responsible for the observed improvement in mechanical performance. Fig. 7 TEM images of alloy 7075 showing the evolution of the density of hardening precipitates:  a  S1,  b  S2,  c  S4, and  d  S5

To support the present funding a schematic time–temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram for AA7075 is given in Fig.  8 : This diagram illustrates the precipitation sequence from a supersaturated  α -Al solid solution to Guinier–Preston (GP) zones, followed by the metastable  η ′ phase and finally the equilibrium  η  (MgZn 2 ) phase. At lower temperatures (~ 100–120 °C), fine GP zones dominate, contributing to peak hardness as in the T6 temper. With increasing temperature or prolonged aging (~ 140–180 °C), transformation to  η ′ and subsequently coarser  η  precipitates occur, characteristic of T7x tempers, which improve corrosion resistance at the expense of strength. Fig. 8 Schematic TTT diagram for AA7075 alloy showing the precipitation sequence from supersaturated  α -Al solid solution to GP zones,  η ′, and equilibrium  η  (MgZn 2 ) phases, highlighting T6, T7x, and sequential tempering paths for optimized mechanical and corrosion properties

The sequential tempering path, involving controlled heating between these regimes, promotes a high density of finely distributed  η ′ precipitates while limiting over-aging, thereby achieving an optimized balance between mechanical strength and corrosion resistance. This schematic supports the observed microstructural evolution and property enhancement reported in the present study.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The current study examined how the heating rise rate affected the Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy microstructure and mechanical properties. The plastic and hardening properties were investigated using tensile and microhardness tests. The microstructural evolution was examined using transmission and scanning electron microscopy. In addition, differential scanning calorimetry was employed to identify the thermal stability and transformation sequence of precipitates. During two-stage tempering, the Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy displayed noticeable changes in microstructure and mechanical behavior. Upon quenching, the microstructure exhibited high ductility. When the alloy is aged at 140 °C, the maximum hardness value, of approximately 240–242 HV, a high-volume fraction of fine precipitates, is apparent. The minimum hardening is recorded after aging at 350 °C. The higher value of yield strength of the samples given the two-step aging is due to the higher precipitate fraction volume, giving rise to a smaller inter-precipitate spacing, and thus, a higher stress is required for dislocation bowing, as reflected by the increases in yield strength from 496.75 MPa (S1) to approximately 607–618 MPa (S4–S6). The decrease in the rate of heating can gradually increase the yield strength values until reaching their saturation, which is observed around 20 °C h −1  (S4), beyond which further reduction in heating rate results in changes within the experimental scatter (± 10 MPa). Indeed, the comparison between samples S 1  (aged at 140 °C) and S 5  (aged at 105 °C and at 140 °C at a heating rate of 20 °C h −1 ) shows that the yield stress increases by 122.06 MPa and the elongation decreases by 0.59%, confirming a significant strengthening effect with only a slight reduction in ductility (from 18.21 to 17.5%). So, a suitable compromise between the two concepts: elongation and yield strength. Moreover, a sufficient nucleation of  η ′ can be achieved as the heating rate decreases, which is supported by DSC results showing precipitation reactions associated with GP zones formation (~ 100–150 °C) and  η ′ phase precipitation (~ 200 °C), and as a result, the improvement in mechanical properties is also very significant, within the investigated conditions. The DSC analysis further confirms the precipitation sequence (GP zones →  η ′ →  η ) and the associated dissolution and reprecipitation process, proving thermal support to the proposed microstructural evolution during tempering (105–140 °C, with a brief exploration at 350 °C). In addition, further investigations involving DSC analyses on tempered samples as well as complementary X-ray diffraction should be undertaken in future work to provide more direct and quantitative confirmation of the precipitation mechanisms.
